name: Corteva, Inc.

profile.description: On October 1, 2026, Corteva completed the spin-off of its seed and genetics business as Vylor Inc. and now operates as a pure-play global crop protection company under the CTVA ticker. Its products include herbicides ($3.73B of FY2025 sales), insecticides ($1.67B), fungicides ($1.14B) and biologicals ($519M). Luke Kissam, former chairman and CEO of Albemarle, became CEO at separation; former CEO Chuck Magro now leads Vylor. On a carve-out basis the crop protection business had FY2025 net sales of $7.84B and net income of $570M, and first-half 2026 sales were $3.85B, up 3.2%. The post-spin stock trades near $11.47, a market cap of about $7.7B.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): Corteva has built biologicals into a $519M revenue line within crop protection (FY2025) and positions the new company around a 'first-mover advantage in nature-inspired technologies.' The October 2026 separation into a pure-play crop protection company is itself a major strategic reshaping [3][5]. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI-powered crop protection products or quantified AI-driven savings were found [5]. Market Share (1/2): Corteva is a top-tier global crop protection supplier with $7.84B of carve-out sales, but Q2 2026 organic crop protection sales fell 1% and price fell 3% under Latin American competition, so there is no evidence of share leadership or gains [1][4]. Pipeline (1/2): New products drove 2% volume growth in Q2 2026, and management describes the company as 'innovation-driven,' but no named next-generation launches with revenue targets were found [4][5]. R&D Intensity (0/1): Carve-out R&D of $479M (6.1% of FY2025 sales) has edged down from $496M in 2023 and is not top-quartile for agrochemicals [1].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Corteva's purpose of enriching the lives of those who produce and consume food, now focused on crop protection, clearly links its products to farmer productivity and food supply [5]. It is not yet a distinctive purpose for the newly separated company. Community Impact (0/2): No distinctive, quantified community or foundation program for the new Corteva was found. Employee Retention (0/2): The company is going through a major organizational disruption, with a corporate split, an outside CEO hired from Albemarle and leadership teams divided between two companies. No retention data was found [5]. Insider Buying (0/2): No meaningful net insider buying was found.

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on the Growth sleeve formula using post-spin crop protection carve-out financials. The pre-spin dividend of $0.18 a quarter yielded only about 0.9%, and no post-spin dividend policy has been confirmed [4]. D/E of 57.4% ($4.77B of debt against $8.32B of Corteva equity at June 30, 2026) scores 1.0 [2]. TTM ROE of 5.7% (about $476M of net income attributable to Corteva) scores 0.38 at 2x weight. Revenue growth of 3.2% (H1 2026 $3.851B vs $3.731B) scores 0.77, and the TTM net margin of 6.0% scores 0.30 [1][2]. Forward P/E, forward PEG and the 5-year revenue CAGR are excluded as unavailable. Consensus estimates in the data feed have not been rebased for the spin-off, and carve-out history covers only 2023 to 2025, when sales went from $8.07B to $7.84B (about -1.4% a year) [1]. Weighted sum is 2.83 of 5, which rounds to 6. Liquidity is about $390M a day [7].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (6/9): Crop protection chemistry and biologicals are physical, heavily regulated products (each active ingredient requires years of registration data), and AI cannot substitute for them in the field [1]. AI-driven precision agriculture does pose a real volume risk. Computer-vision spot-spraying and variable-rate application can sharply reduce herbicide use per acre, and herbicides are Corteva's largest category at $3.73B, nearly half of crop protection sales [3]. AI-accelerated molecule discovery could also lower barriers for rivals and generic producers. No analyst commentary quantifying this risk was found. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI-related revenue is disclosed [5].

infinite_game.summary: Corteva has just made a dramatic structural move by separating seed from crop protection, with an outside CEO and a promise of an 'innovation-driven, asset-light' model. Through Sinek's lens, a breakup aimed at unlocking valuation is a finite-game tool unless it serves a deeper cause, and the new company has not yet stated or tested one. Legacy chlorpyrifos and PFAS liabilities, along with an FTC antitrust suit, weigh on how stakeholders perceive it.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Helping farmers protect crops and feed a growing world is a service-oriented aim, and the 'nature-inspired technologies' strategy and $519M biologicals business give it some substance [3][5]. The newly independent company has not yet shown it holds the purpose through hard times, and the separation was framed largely in value-creation terms.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Corteva announced the executive teams for both companies months before the October 2026 separation, which gave employees clarity during the split [5]. The new CEO is an outsider, Luke Kissam from Albemarle, and no engagement or turnover data was found, so this scores as adequate rather than high-trust.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Management commentary attributes Q2 2026 price declines to 'market dynamics in Latin America' and generic competition [4]. No acknowledgment of rivals' strengths as a spur to improvement was found, and the FTC and ten state attorneys general sued Corteva in 2022 over alleged anticompetitive conduct [6].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Corteva split off its larger seed business (Vylor) and is betting on biologicals and nature-inspired chemistry [3][5]. It also stopped producing Lorsban (chlorpyrifos) in 2020 amid health concerns [6]. These are meaningful adaptations, but the separation restructures rather than reinvents what crop protection does, so it earns partial credit.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Exiting Lorsban production in 2020 gave up an established product line, and the decision to separate into two focused companies took on significant dis-synergy and execution risk, including a $25M dis-synergy headwind in 2026 guidance [4][6]. R&D spending has drifted down from $496M to $479M since 2023, so there is no pattern of costly long-term investment [1].

investment_thesis: The new Corteva is a focused, global crop protection franchise with $7.84B of FY2025 carve-out sales, a diversified portfolio (herbicides $3.73B, insecticides $1.67B, fungicides $1.14B) and a growing $519M biologicals platform [1][3]. Profitability is recovering: carve-out net income went from a $185M loss in 2023 and a $25M loss in 2024 to $570M of profit in 2025 [1]. Before the spin, management raised full-year 2026 guidance to $4.1B to $4.3B of operating EBITDA, and new-product volume grew 2% in Q2 [4]. At about $7.7B of market cap and roughly 16x TTM earnings, with D/E of 57%, the stock gives the incoming Albemarle-veteran CEO room to pursue the stated 'asset-light, innovation-driven' model and margin expansion [2][5].
thesis_continued: The bear case starts with growth and pricing. Carve-out sales fell from $8.07B in 2023 to $7.84B in 2025, and in Q2 2026 crop protection organic sales fell 1% as price dropped 3% under Latin American and generic competition [1][4]. Profitability is thin: TTM net margin is about 6% and ROE about 5.7%, and H1 2026 net income fell to $157M from $241M [2]. Short-term borrowings jumped to $3.09B by June 2026 as the balance sheet was reset for separation, and equity fell from $11.4B to $8.3B [2]. Legacy liabilities remain: chlorpyrifos personal-injury claims, pending PFAS suits from legacy DuPont (including New Jersey and East Hampton), and the 2022 FTC antitrust case [6]. The Inspire Impact Score of -49 (MISALIGNED) is a further issue for faith-based mandates.
key_catalysts: First standalone quarterly report and refreshed post-spin guidance from CEO Luke Kissam, setting margin, capital allocation and dividend policy for the pure-play crop protection company [3][5]
Growth of the $519M biologicals business and 'nature-inspired' products, which drove 2% Q2 2026 volume growth despite price pressure [3][4]
Asset-light operating model and dis-synergy offsets; management said net dis-synergies are largely offset on a run-rate basis, with only a $25M headwind in 2026 [4]
key_risks: Generic and Latin American pricing pressure: Q2 2026 crop protection price fell 3% and organic sales fell 1% [4]
Legacy litigation: chlorpyrifos personal-injury claims, remaining PFAS suits after the 2024 public-water settlement, and the 2022 FTC and state antitrust case [6]
Precision agriculture volume risk: AI-enabled spot spraying could structurally cut herbicide volume per acre, threatening the $3.73B herbicide franchise [3]
